## Creative challenge

Design your own piece of climate data art using the same dataset.

You are free to experiment with geometric shapes, color palettes, transparency, repetition, coordinate transformations, and visual composition.

Create an original visualization using `ggplot2` and the NASA GISTEMP dataset.

Your artwork should satisfy three requirements:

1. It must be generated programmatically from the dataset, rather than manually illustrated.
2. At least one visual property (color, size, position, shape, or opacity) must encode a numerical variable.
3. The visual composition must communicate a meaningful aspect of global warming.

You may remove conventional statistical elements such as axes, titles, legends, and labels, but you must document how the data are mapped to the artwork.


### Setup
```{r}

library(tidyverse)

url <- paste0(
  "https://data.giss.nasa.gov/gistemp/",
  "tabledata_v4/GLB.Ts+dSST.csv"
)

temp_raw <- read_csv(
  url,
  skip = 1,
  na = c("***", "****"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

```

```{r}
temp <- temp_raw |>
  select(Year, Jan:Dec) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = Jan:Dec,
    names_to = "month",
    values_to = "anomaly"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(month, levels = month.abb),
    date = as.Date(
      paste(Year, month, "01", sep = "-"),
      format = "%Y-%b-%d"
    )
  ) |>
  drop_na(anomaly)

head(temp, n = 12)

```


### Climate data art: *The Climate Sunflower*

Instead of a traditional time series, rectangular grid, or circular spiral, we can arrange monthly temperature anomalies using **phyllotaxis**: 
the mathematical pattern found in sunflowers and other botanical structures.

Each observation is placed outward from the center using the **golden angle** ($\approx 137.5^\circ$).
So we can see older months (from 1880) in the core of the flower, while recent years are at the outer edge.

```{r}
golden_angle <- pi * (3 - sqrt(5))

sunflower <- temp |>
  arrange(Year, month) |>
  mutate(
    n = row_number(),
    angle = n * golden_angle,
    radius = sqrt(n),
    x = radius * cos(angle),
    y = radius * sin(angle)
  )

art_plot <- ggplot(sunflower, aes(
  x = x,
  y = y,
  color = anomaly,
  size = anomaly
)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.85) +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_color_gradient2(
    low = "#2166AC",
    mid = "#F7F7F7",
    high = "#B2182B",
    midpoint = 0
  ) +
  scale_size_continuous(
    range = c(0.6, 3.2),
    guide = "none"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "The Climate Sunflower",
    subtitle = "Monthly global temperature anomalies (1880–present)",
    color = "°C",
  ) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 15, hjust = 0.5),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 10, hjust = 0.5, color = "grey30"),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8, hjust = 0.5, color = "grey50"),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

art_plot

ggsave(
  filename = "climate_sunflower.png",
  plot = art_plot,
  width = 8,
  height = 8,
  dpi = 300,
  bg = "white"
)
```

- `golden_angle` defines the Fibonacci golden angle: $\pi(3 - \sqrt{5})$.
- `n = row_number()` assigns a chronological index to each month from 1880 to the present.
- `angle` rotates each successive month by one golden angle, while radius = sqrt(n) places later observations progressively farther from the center.
- `x` and `y` convert the polar coordinates (radius, angle) into Cartesian coordinates.
- `geom_point()` draws one seed per month, encoding the temperature anomaly through both **color** (color = anomaly) and **size** (size = anomaly).
- `coord_equal()` preserves the circular symmetry of the phyllotaxis pattern.
- `scale_color_gradient2()` uses the diverging blue–white–red climate palette centered at 0°C.
- `theme_void()` removes axes and gridlines.
- `ggsave()` exports the final artwork.
